You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Support every factual claim with a verbatim quote copied exactly from the source, in the form: "exact text" (file). Never paraphrase inside the quotation marks. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no citation.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- Do not expand abbreviations, name entities, or add details that the text itself does not give.
- Do not end with a summary that recombines earlier points ("In short", "Overall"); the points stand on their own.
- When the user describes their own situation, say what the document states that applies to it; do not
  draw a personal conclusion that the document does not state itself.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

352	Informal financial services
   353	2.1 Introduction
   354	In recent years research into informal financial services and systems has significantly deepened
   355	understanding of the way they operate and their strengths and weaknesses. A simplistic belief that
   356	local money-lenders charged extortionate interest rates lay behind the provision of subsidised
   357	finance in the past. More thorough investigation has highlighted a range of savings, credit, and
   358	insurance facilities accessible to poor people. The appar- ently usurious interest charges
   359	reportedly made by private money-lenders may be explainable in terms of transaction costs, lack of
   360	information, and high risk. Informal financial services may be well-equipped, because of local
   361	'insider' knowledge, and lower overheads, to respond to the requirements of poor people; they may
   362	also be exploitative.
   363	This chapter starts with a brief overview of the types of informal services that have been found to
   364	exist in a wide variety of countries and social contexts. Some of the broad characteristics of these
   365	services are identified, and lessons drawn for the design of NGO or semi-formal systems. In describ-
   366	ing informal financial services it is useful to distinguish between those which are owned by their
   367	users and those which are offered by an individual, usually on a profit-making basis. The
   368	distinction can be a helpful one in analysing the ways in which financial services enable or exploit
   369	poor people. NGOs considering microfinance interventions need first to find out what informal
   370	financial services are available, and how they operate. Such services are capable of supporting poor
   371	people's livelihoods as well as perpetuating
   372	1 This chapter draws heavily on a background paper commissioned for the purposes of this book: A
   373	Critical Typology of Financial Services for the Poor, Stuart Rutherford, November 1996. Examples are
   374	drawn from Rutherford's own experience unless otherwise stated.
   375	16
   376	Informal financial services
   377	structures which undermine them. It is necessary, therefore, to understand under what circumstances
   378	and to what degree these services are enabling or exploitative for poor people. On the whole,
   379	user-owned services are likely to be more enabling than services provided for profit.
   380	Investigating the scope and nature of existing services is an essential pre- liminary before
   381	considering whether an intervention is necessary. However, NGOs themselves may not have the right
   382	skills to become direct providers of financial services. Furthermore, financial services are needed
   383	by poor people on a permanent basis to enable them to plan and manage their finances; NGO programmes
   384	which might be here today and gone tomorrow may be an inap- propriate means through which to provide
   385	them. Therefore NGOs should seriously consider whether direct intervention is in fact the best
   386	response for them to make. The chapter closes by discussing alternative strategies NGOs might
   387	employ.
   388	2.2 User-owned informal financial services
   389	Systems which facilitate financial transactions and are owned by their users are many and varied,
   390	and range from simple reciprocal arrangements between neighbours, savings clubs and rotating savings
   391	and credit associa- tions (ROSCAS), to forms of insurance, building societies, and systems of co-
   392	operative business finance. An example of each of these types is described below. All of these
   393	systems can be found in a variety of country settings.
   394	Rotating savings and credit associations (ROSCAS) in particular, are an extremely common phenomenon.
   395	They exist in almost every country (for example, 'partners' in Jamaica and Britain, bui in Vietnam,
   396	and njangi in Cameroon). (See Bouman, 1995; Ardener and Burman, 1995 for detailed and extensive
   397	surveys of ROSCA operations in a range of settings.) The principle is very simple: a number of
   398	people agree to save a fixed amount of money at regular intervals; at each meeting, for example
   399	weekly, each member contri- butes an agreed amount, resulting in a single lump sum becoming
   400	available, which is then allocated to one of the members. There are three basic varia- tions in the
   401	way in which this lump sum or 'prize' is allocated. First, it can be allocated on the basis of
   402	strict rotation between members of the group; second, on the basis of a lottery of members; third,
   403	it may be auctioned to the member who is willing to accept the biggest discount. The group will
   404	usually meet (but does not always need to) and undertake this transaction on as many occasions as
   405	there are members of the group, thus ensuring that each member gets the 'prize' once. The ROSCA
   406	demonstrates the basic principle of financial intermediation: collecting many small savings from
   407	many people, turning this into a lump sum for one person, and repeating this procedure over time.
   408	17
   409	Microfinance and Poverty Reduction
   410	ROSCA finance is used for many purposes. Some ROSCAS operate to enable an asset to be purchased,
   411	such as a rickshaw or fishing equipment for each member, and may have been set up specifically for
   412	the purpose. 'Merry- go-rounds', as ROSCAS are called among Kikuyu women in Kenya, are sometimes
   413	used by women as a means of accumulating enough money to buy new household utensils or clothes. The
   414	technology of the ROSCA is not unique to poor communities but is also used by salaried professionals
   415	to purchase major consumption items or assets such as refrigerators or cars.
   416	A further example of a user-owned device is the insurance fund which makes pay-outs conditional on
   417	certain circumstances occurring. These are int- ended to cover large expenses such as those
   418	connected with marriage or death.
   419	2.2.1 Some examples of user-owned financial services
   420	Neighbourhood reciprocity in Southern India Reciprocal lending may be extended to involve several or
   421	even all the members of a community. Among Moslems in Kerala State in southern India kuri kalyanam
   422	are invitations to a feast to which the guest is expected to bring a cash gift. When the host in his
   423	turn is invited to a feast by one of the guests he is expected to return double the amount (less if
   424	he is perceived as poor). In Vietnam one kind of hui (a generic name for various financial devices)
   425	involves a similar pooling of resources for one person on one occasion to be reciprocated later by
   426	others, at different times.
   427	Rickshaw ROSCAS in Bangladesh
   428	Very poor men driven by poverty from their home villages to the Bangladesh capital, Dhaka, often
   429	earn a living there by driving bired rickshaws. In the last ten years they have begun to run ROSCAS.
   430	A group of drivers forms, and each driver saves a set amount from his daily takings. When the fund
   431	is large enough (this usually takes about 15 days) a rickshaw is bought and distributed by lottery
   432	to one of the members. In between prizes' the cash is held by a trustworthy outsider, usually a
   433	local shopkeeper from whom the members buy their tea or cigarettes. In a further adaptation, those
   434	who have already received their rickshaw double their daily contribution. This progressively reduces
   435	the time-gap between prizes, and is seen as a fair way of rewarding those members who win the
   436	lottery late in the cycle, because their gross contribution is smaller than earlier winners. The
   437	extra payment made by the winners is roughly equivalent to what they save by no longer having to
   438	hire a rickshaw.

440	An accumulating savings club in Mexico
   441	Informal financial services
   442	In towns and villages in Mexico neighbours place frequent but irregular savings with trusted
   443	shopkeepers. Just before Christmas, the cash is returned to the saver. No interest is paid, but the
   444	saver has a lump sum to spend, and the shopkeeper has had the use of the money over the year and can
   445	now look forward to a good sales season.
   446	Building societies for the middle classes in Bangladesh In a lower-middle-class area of Dhaka, 165
   447	employees in the Public Works Department belong to their own building society' which was started
   448	over 16 years ago. Each saves 200 taka ($5) a month out of his wages. As the cash accumulates it is
   449	lent out to members, who buy land and building materials. Interest rates are high and interest on
   450	the out- standing balance has to be paid each month, to encourage modest loans and rapid repayment.
   451	But loan sizes are generous and such workers would have few or no alternative sources for loans of
   452	this kind.
   453	Popular insurance: funeral funds (iddir) in Ethiopia
   454	Originally burial societies, iddir have extended to provide a wide range of insurance services in
   455	urban Ethiopia. Aredo (1993), study- ing these in Addis Ababa, estimated that 50 per cent of urban
   456	house- holds were members of some kind of iddir. Groups of people come together on the basis of
   457	location, occupation, friendship or family ties. Each iddir sets its own rules and regulations but
   458	usually pays out for funeral expenses or financial assistance to families of the deceased, and
   459	sometimes to cover other costs, such as medical expenses and losses due to fire or theft.
   460	2.3 Informal financial services for profit
   461	Those offering informal financial services for profit fall into two groups: deposit takers (often
   462	also called money-guards) and lenders.
   463	What is most interesting about the situation of deposit takers is that, as in the Nigerian example
   464	below, savers usually pay for the service by obtaining a negative interest rate on their funds. This
   465	demonstrates the pressing need that people have for places to put their savings which are safe and
   466	secure not only from physical risks such as theft, fire or flood, but also from the demands of their
   467	family. For women, in particular, the ability to save small amounts in places to which their
   468	husbands and families cannot gain access (although they might know about them) has been shown to be
   469	particularly important. It may enable them to meet obligations in the family or household, such as
   470	the payment of children's school fees, for which they have particular responsibility.
   471	19
   472	Microfinance and Poverty Reduction
   473	Forms of lending also operate in a variety of ways, such as money-lenders; pawnbrokers, who take
   474	collateral in the form of physical assets; and forms of trade credit and hire purchase. The term
   475	'money-lender' can cause confusion because it conjures up the image of a class of people whose main
   476	source of income is usury. In reality, many small farmers, for example, obtain credit from
   477	employers, landlords, traders, relatives, and other people who combine a number of economic
   478	activities. In some places money-lenders may be a more professionalised class, such as the
   479	Tamilians' in Cochin described below, but even in this case it is not necessarily their main source
   480	of income.
   481	Lending money can be exploitative of, as well as enabling for, poor people. People facing seasonal
   482	shortages may have only one source of credit, for example, an employer. The employer may agree to
   483	provide a loan, but only if the borrower promises to work when required at below the going
   484	wage-rate. As described below for Indonesia, crop traders may provide producers with seasonal credit
   485	on the understanding that the crop is sold through the same trader at low post-harvest prices. Tied
   486	credit of this type, whether in cash or kind, may be the only means of survival for poor people. But
   487	arrangements such as these can maintain and even exacerbate inequalities in power and position. In
   488	contrast, user-owned devices are likely to be more supportive and enabling, because the profits made
   489	are pooled, and shared or fed back into the system, and ownership and control of the funds are in
   490	the hands of the users. Such devices are unlikely to be exploitative of those involved, although
   491	they may widen inequalities between users and non-users. The comparison with services for profit is
   492	clear.
   493	However, loans from private lenders after harvest may enable small traders to make the most of the
   494	increased liquidity in the local economy. This emphasises the need for interveners to understand the
   495	workings of real markets and to question untested assumptions. It is essential to find out for which
   496	groups of poor people-women, men, landless labourers, subsistence farmers, migrant workers and under
   497	what circumstances these arrange- ments may be no more than a means of survival, while supporting
   498	wealth creation for others.
   499	2.3.1 Some examples of informal financial services provided for profit
   500	Deposit takers: a mobile alajo in Nigeria
   501	One consequence of Nigeria's current political difficulties is a drop in public confidence in formal
   502	banks, according to Gemini News. This has allowed an old tradition to flourish again- alajos, or
   503	peripatetic deposit takers. Idowu Alakpere uses a bicycle to go
   504	20
   505	Informal financial services
   506	door-to-door round the outer suburb of Lagos where he lives. He has
   507	500 customers who each save about 10 or 15 naira with him (about 50 to 75 cents US) at each daily
   508	visit. Customers withdraw money whenever they like, and Idowu charges them one day's savings per
   509	month, which he deducts from the withdrawal. Since deposits are made evenly over the month, the
   510	negative interest rate for one-month deposits is 1/15, or 6.6 per cent a month, an Annual Percentage
   511	Rate (APR) of 80 per cent. Some alajos, including Idowu, store the cash in a reliable bank, others
   512	use it to make loans. The Gemini News reporter was told by many local people that they trusted these
   513	alajos more than banks. When it was pointed out that some alajos are dishonest, they retorted that
   514	so are many banks.
   515	Professional money-lenders in Cochin, India
   516	'Tamilians' provide a money-lending service to poor slum dwellers on a daily basis. They have set
   517	terms, which are well-known all over Cochin. For each 100 rupees lent, 3 rupees are deducted at
   518	source as a fee. Thereafter, 12.50 rupees per week must be repaid for ten weeks. This works out at
   519	an APR of 300 per cent (28 rupees paid on an average size loan of 48.50 rupees [97/2) for 10/52 of a
   520	year). Most non-poor observers regard this rate as outrageously exploitative. However, poor users of
   521	the service tend to take a favourable view of it. The 'Tamilians' do not needlessly harass their
   522	clients over repay- ment but take an 'understanding' view which includes a willingness to accept
   523	loan losses. These money-lenders know their clients well and (out of self-interest) will not lend
   524	more than they think the client can repay out of normal income over the next ten weeks.

   526	their local pawnbroker when they need money quickly. He is reliably available at his gold- smithing
   527	shop and he charges 3 per cent a month for loans pledged against gold, 5 per cent for silver and 9

   543	Two examples of trade credit
   544	In many markets it is common to see poor people squatting on the ground with a small amount of
   545	fertiliser spread out on a mat. The fertiliser doesn't necessarily belong to the man or woman (or,
   546	often, child). Lacking capital themselves to buy stock, such people obtain the fertiliser on credit
   547	from a nearby shop. At the close of the market they return the money from sales and any balance of
   548	the stock to the shopkeeper, retaining a small proportion of the money. The system allows people to
   549	trade (safely if not profitably) without capital, and gives the shopkeeper a cheap extra outlet.
   550	The dadon credit system used to finance prawn cultivation in Bangladesh is an example of a trading
   551	system in which credit is passed on through a chain of intermediaries between the prawn farmer and
   552	exporters to Europe. The prawn market is a highly com- petitive business in which everyone in the
   553	chain is short of capital. The 'commission agent' at the port buys prawns on behalf of the exporters
   554	in the capital. To ensure their share of the market they provide credit early in the season which
   555	finds its way through a number of intermediaries before reaching the hands of the farmer. The
   556	intermediaries are 'depot' owners, then farias', or merchants, and finally local traders, who in
   557	turn lend to the farmers. In accepting the credit the farmer commits himself to selling exclusively
   558	to this particular trader.
